mainTopic: Can sanctity end by itself, with no פדיון? The difference between קדושת דמים and קדושת הגוף
overview: This amud continues the discussion of the משנה's case of saplings declared holy until they are cut. רב המנונא asks how such holiness can simply disappear. He compares it to a marriage, which cannot end without a גט. רבא answers by separating two kinds of holiness. קדושת דמים, holiness of monetary value, can end by itself. קדושת הגוף, holiness of the thing itself, cannot. אביי challenges רבא with a ברייתא about an ox that is an עולה for thirty days and a שלמים afterward. The גמרא answers that the man consecrated only the ox's value, so it was קדושת דמים. The גמרא then tests this answer against the end of the same ברייתא, where the order of the offerings is flipped, and that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Where did the sanctity go?
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא challenges the idea that the saplings' sanctity disappears on its own, comparing it to a woman who cannot leave a marriage without a גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said to him: Their holiness, where did it go? If a man told a woman, 'Today you are my wife and tomorrow you are not my wife,' would she leave the marriage without a גט?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא is attacking the claim that the saplings become non-holy by themselves once they are cut. He asks how holiness can simply disappear with no פדיון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His comparison is קידושין. A man cannot make a marriage that ends by itself on a set date, because a marriage only ends through a גט. In the same way, once something becomes holy, its holiness should need an action, like פדיון, to remove it.

keyTerms.meaning: Holiness, sanctity
Where did it go?
A bill of divorce
She goes out, she leaves the marriage

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" is עולא, who said the saplings lose their holiness once they are cut.

phrases.english: The holiness that was in them, where did it go?
And what if one said to a woman
"Today you are my wife
and tomorrow you are not my wife,"
would she leave without a bill of divorce?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges עולא's earlier ruling about the saplings, which comes just before this part of the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the saplings' holiness ends by itself when they are cut
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A status like marriage cannot end automatically. It needs a גט. So holiness should also need פדיון to end.
steps.whyThisMatters: This question sets up the key distinction of the whole sugya: are all kinds of holiness alike?

steps.title: Two kinds of holiness
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the saplings have קדושת דמים, which can end by itself. A wife's status is like קדושת הגוף, which cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Are you comparing holiness of value to holiness of the body itself? Holiness of value can end with nothing done. Holiness of the body does not end with nothing done.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends the ruling about the saplings by showing that רב המנונא's comparison does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saplings are holy only for their money value (קדושת דמים), and that kind of holiness can end on its own when its condition is met. A wife is like קדושת הגוף, where the person or thing itself takes on the status, and that can only be removed by an action. So the marriage case proves nothing about the saplings.

keyTerms.meaning: Holiness of monetary value. The item is holy only for what it is worth.
Inherent holiness. The thing itself is holy.
It departs, it falls away
For nothing, without any action being done
You compare

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the saplings were never holy. They really were holy, but only with קדושת דמים, and that kind of holiness is able to end by itself.
steps.whatToRemember: קדושת דמים can end without any action. קדושת הגוף needs an action to end it.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
Are you comparing sanctity of monetary value
to inherent sanctity?
Sanctity of value departs with nothing being done,
inherent sanctity does not depart with nothing being done.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי קָא מְדַמֵּית קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים לִקְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב המנונא's challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All holiness works like marriage, so it can never end by itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only קדושת הגוף needs an action to end. קדושת דמים, like the saplings, can end on its own.
steps.whyThisMatters: The difference between קדושת דמים and קדושת הגוף comes up again and again in הקדש topics across ש״ס.

steps.title: The ox that changes from עולה to שלמים
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבא with a ברייתא where an animal's קדושת הגוף seems to change by itself after thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Inherent holiness does not end with nothing done? But a ברייתא teaches: 'This ox is an עולה for thirty days, and after thirty days it is a שלמים.' And the ruling is that for thirty days it is an עולה, and after thirty days a שלמים. Why? Offerings have inherent holiness, and here it ended with nothing done!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's rule that קדושת הגוף cannot end by itself, using a ברייתא as a counter-example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal set aside as a קרבן normally has קדושת הגוף. Yet the ברייתא says its status as an עולה ends automatically after thirty days, and it becomes a שלמים with no action taken. That seems to show that קדושת הגוף can end by itself, which goes against רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: A burnt-offering, burned entirely on the מזבח
A peace-offering, mostly eaten by the owners
Why?
They are

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
Inherent sanctity does not depart with nothing being done?
But isn't it taught in a baraita:
"This ox is a burnt-offering for all thirty days,
and after thirty days a peace-offering"
for all thirty days it is a burnt-offering,
after thirty days it is a peace-offering.
Why?
These are inherent sanctity,
and it departs with nothing being done!

steps.triggerLanguage: קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף לָא פָּקְעָה בִּכְדִי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule רבא set up in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that קדושת הגוף never ends with nothing done
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An offering's holiness is קדושת הגוף, yet in the ברייתא the עולה status ends automatically after thirty days.

steps.title: He consecrated only the ox's value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about someone who consecrated only the ox's monetary value, so it was קדושת דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where he said he was consecrating it for its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא by explaining the ברייתא as a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the man consecrated only the ox's value, to buy an עולה and later a שלמים with it, then the ox never had קדושת הגוף. It had only קדושת דמים, which can change by itself. So the ברייתא fits רבא's rule after all.

keyTerms.meaning: With what are we dealing here? (narrows a source to a specific case)
For its monetary value

steps.whatToRemember: According to this answer, the ox case is about consecrating only its value (קדושת דמים), so it does not contradict רבא's rule that קדושת הגוף does not end by itself. The next step challenges this answer.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
Where he said it was for its monetary value.
phrases.notes: He means the ox's value would be used to buy the offerings. The ox itself was never set aside to be offered.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ox in the ברייתא had קדושת הגוף, and its holiness changed by itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ox had only קדושת דמים, so its status could change with nothing done, just as רבא said.

steps.title: Testing the answer against the second half of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 4. It quotes the סיפא of the ברייתא, where the ox is an עולה after thirty days and a שלמים until then. It starts arguing that things make sense only if one clause is קדושת הגוף and the other is קדושת דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the end of the ברייתא: 'After thirty days it is an עולה, and from now it is a שלמים.' Granted, if you say one clause is about קדושת הגוף and the other is about קדושת דמים, then...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a challenge to the last answer by quoting the second half of the ברייתא. It begins a 'granted, if...' argument that is finished on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said the ברייתא is about קדושת דמים, which can end by itself. The גמרא now points to the סיפא, which flips the order of עולה and שלמים. It suggests the ברייתא makes sense if its two clauses deal with two different kinds of קדושה, which would mean not everything in it is קדושת דמים.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. It takes the last answer and tests what follows from it.
Say the end clause. Look at the later part of the same source.
A burnt-offering, which is burned completely on the מזבח.
A peace-offering, whose meat is mostly eaten by the owners.
Granted, if you say. It opens an 'this works if...' argument that sets up a contrast.

steps.confusionAlert: This step ends in the middle of a sentence. The 'granted, if you say' is only the first half of the argument, and the challenge is completed on the next amud.

phrases.english: If so, say the latter clause:
"After thirty days, a burnt-offering,
and from now, a peace-offering."
Granted, if you say
that one clause is about inherent sanctity,
and one clause is about sanctity of monetary value —
phrases.notes: The sentence isn't finished yet. The גמרא completes the thought at the start of the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 4's answer that the ברייתא is about קדושת דמים by bringing in the ברייתא's second clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 4 that the ברייתא deals only with consecrating the ox's money value (קדושת דמים).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second half of the ברייתא flips the order of the offerings. The גמרא suggests the ברייתא makes sense if one clause is about קדושת הגוף and the other about קדושת דמים, which would weaken the claim that it is all קדושת דמים. The full argument is completed on the next amud.
